At a first glance, one might think that Team Fortress 2 (referred to as TF2), is a completely and utterly stupid game and should never be played. Sure, throwing urine at people and then sniping them (sometimes at the same time) might sound a little strange, but it's exceptionally fun to do. Seriously.
Who WOULDN'T like a Bostonian running around shouting random remarks at the other team? He also throws milk at people and hits people with baseball bats.
The embodiment of America, this completely insane Not-Actually-A-Soldier is often found firing off rockets and hitting people with shovels. He also can fire rockets his feet to jump very high. Then he hits people with shovels.
This class is of the great unknown. No one knows what they look like. No one knows what sex/gender they are. No one knows what they're saying half the time, but despite all these attributes, the Pyro can still set people on fire. Which may or may not be a good thing.
The master of explosives (and swords...?) can fire off explosive pills (PILLS HERE) that do exactly what's on the tin; explode. Luckily, he's also got spiked bombs that he can remotely detonate. What could make this class any better? He's drunk.
The face of TF2, he is a giant. He's got a minigun, a shotgun, and his fists (which do the same amount of damage as a fire axe), so he's pretty indestructible. Oh, and he can replace his shotgun for a sandwich. What a great trade!
This Texan places down a sentry that is basically a mix of the Heavy's minigun, and the Soldier's rocket launcher. He can also make a vending machine that will heal, give ammo, and block enemy players. AND THERE'S MORE! He can also place down teleporters that can get teammates to the front lines quickly. Tip: do NOT teleport bread. Especially for three days.
This German mad scientist has a tendency to shoot people with syringes to make them die. Or to heal his teammates. Or to heal himself. It doesn't really matter what he does, but he'll do it FOR SCIENCE. Also, he has a big old tube that heals people for no cost. After a bit of time, it will be able to initiate GOD MODE *cough* I mean the Übercharge, which prevents all incoming damage.
The Australian who is actually from New Zealand, The Sniper shoots people in the head with his sniper rifle, and if that doesn't kill them, shoots them with an SMG. And if THAT doesn't work, he throws urine at them, then cuts them with a Kukri that for some reason can do more damage then his sniper rifle. Overall, he's a pretty cool guy.
Espionage has never been simpler, when you can
Overall, this game is a blast. Literally and metaphorically. I recommend this to anyone and everyone who plays on Steam. If you don't play on Steam, make an account, download Steam, download TF2, and then play TF2. It's pretty simple.

TF2 is often and rightly called the premiere combat-themed millinery and haberdashery simulator.
However, this belies its simple, corrupting nature. Do not underestimate the power of this aged wonder to enthrall you, coddling you safely in its free entertainment clutches, where you will discover orgiastic bliss in the merciless and frenzied slaughter of your fellow hat mannequins.
Better described as "a teamwork-orientated, objective-based arena FPS", TF2 is perhaps one of the best games currently available for play, despite its age, its 'unrealistic' combat, and its absurd digs at lore, backstory, and continuity.
Why?
Because there is Nothing. Like. It. Go take a look at some high level competitive play for TF2. Watch the classes swoop through the air. This is not Battlefield. This is not Call of Duty. This is old school Quake madness, packaged in small doses and piped directly into your cranium. It's fast, it's frenzied, and it's best played when
, like the team-based modes of arena shooters from years gone by.
Are you a team player? At its peak, TF2 will elate you, as you revel in the victory that only organized teamply will rightly bring you. At its low point, TF2 will infuriate you, as people goof off, fail to organize, and get rolled.
It's free to play, but there's no attempt to force the player into buying mechanically-beneficial items. Every item that's available that affects gameplay is free - random acquisitions over time, or craft your own from those you break down, trade with other players, or buy it off the marketplace - but anything that's mechanically impacting is available to all. There's no pay to win here.
There is, however, a dizzying array of customizations and decorations that can change the average grunt into a proper
(or scout, heavy, etc, etc.) available - also free (but rarer and harder to come by) to make you stand out in a crowd - whether of your friends or enemies!
Go. Hunt. Kill skuls.
...and maybe wear a fancy hat while you do it?

Team Fortress 2, released in 2007 and still going strong towards late 2015.
The game feels like the timeless classics of Unreal Tournament with basic grab-a-class and go-fight objectives and the game modes are very simple, basically an all-out deathmatch with a few varities of gamemodes.
I beleive what really made this game is the fact that it has its own world and its own story, but that story is very clear on a theme and anything that follows afterwards can be made from its sandbox and I feel like the community has learned the spirit of the game enough and the community has even been allowed to keep the game going.
Coming from Valve with a history of games like Half Life, you sit and anxiously wonder what TF2 must be about or what the story is and oddly enough at how great they are at telling stories in games, this games story is simply mercenaries that only wish to kill each other for cash and that's it.
The game has done such a wonderful job creating such a unique universe with such a simple objective in mind that it has blown up into what we have now and it's still going strong almost 9 years later. Valve has a methodology of knowing that  games like this have insanely dedicated fans and that the death of games are when the developers give up on them, so they've unleashed the TF2 workshop where the same very players can design and submit items and weapons to be brought to life into the game if their submissions are picked.
I think that just goes to show why Steam is becoming a more and more popular option than consoles and why Valve has been doing so well, they're honestly one of the few companies I view as succesful captalist that have thrived on good audience relations and I feel like Team Fortress 2 is a momument to just that.

This is a well made, stylized, team based first person shooter. Teamwork is needed to win at higher levels of play, though lone wolfing is fine on lower skill levels such as on most public servers. There are 9 classes to choose from. Each class has unique weapons and abilities that allow each to fulfill a unique roll as part of a larger team. This provides for a challenging and rewarding experience when faced against opponents of similar or better skill levels. The game has an active dev team that continues to release updates to the game that add new content such as weapons or game modes.
At the time of this review, there are two official modes of play: player versus player and 'Mann Versus Machine'.
Player versus player is a mode where one team of players battles against another team of players. Within this mode, there are different types of maps. Each type of map has it's own objective or objectives for each team to achieve.
'Mann Versus Machine' is a mode where a team of up to 6 players battles against waves of bots. Players collect money from destroyed bots. The money is divided equally among players in the team and can be used to purchase upgrades and abilities for the next wave of bots. The pay to play sub-mode, "Mann Up", gives rewards upon completing a "tour".
In addition to the official modes of play, there are several player made mods that introduce other modes of play such as 'Versus Saxton Hale', where a team of players battles against a player playing as a character named Saxton Hale; 'Dodge Ball', where two teams of players playing as Pyros must airblast rockets and other projectiles back and forth in order to stay alive; 'Zombie Mod', where a team of players must make it to the end of the map without dying to zombies that are played by other players; to name just a few of the many player made mods available.
In addition to game play, players will randomly receive free items from the game. Some of the free items given out are weapons, hats and crates. Hats can be worn by a class to change the appearance of that class. Crates can be opened with a key. Keys can be purchased from the Mann Co Store or from the Steam Community Market or traded for from another player. Most crates will list which items can be found within them.
The game has several communities for a player to choose from if a community is what you are looking for. The game is easy to pick up and play, either alone or with friends, yet has a depth of play that will keep you from becoming bored too quickly. The dynamics between the different classes, weapons, play styles, skill levels, modes and maps provides content for many hours of play. I have been playing since November 2007 and I still return to the game on a regular basis.

Team Fortress 2, released in 2007 and still going strong towards late 2015.
The game feels like the timeless classics of Unreal Tournament with basic grab-a-class and go-fight objectives and the game modes are very simple, basically an all-out deathmatch with a few varities of gamemodes.
I beleive what really made this game is the fact that it has its own world and its own story, but that story is very clear on a theme and anything that follows afterwards can be made from its sandbox and I feel like the community has learned the spirit of the game enough and the community has even been allowed to keep the game going.
Coming from Valve with a history of games like Half Life, you sit and anxiously wonder what TF2 must be about or what the story is and oddly enough at how great they are at telling stories in games, this games story is simply mercenaries that only wish to kill each other for cash and that's it.
The game has done such a wonderful job creating such a unique universe with such a simple objective in mind that it has blown up into what we have now and it's still going strong almost 9 years later. Valve has a methodology of knowing that  games like this have insanely dedicated fans and that the death of games are when the developers give up on them, so they've unleashed the TF2 workshop where the same very players can design and submit items and weapons to be brought to life into the game if their submissions are picked.
I think that just goes to show why Steam is becoming a more and more popular option than consoles and why Valve has been doing so well, they're honestly one of the few companies I view as succesful captalist that have thrived on good audience relations and I feel like Team Fortress 2 is a momument to just that.

Even after 10 years, Team Fortress 2 manages to be a really good game and en example for class/hero-based shooters.
Each of the 9 classes provide a unique way to play, and there's a class for everyone. The unlockable weapons also give new ways to play a class (Demoknight, Trolldier, Copterscout, Battle Engi and Battle Med) With over 120 weapons, the battlefield is never one-loadout blanded. (Besides when new class packs come out for 2 days, but anyway...)
Each class can also be customized with cosmetics. These allow you to personalize your favorite classes and make you pop out a little more. There's about 1300 cosmetics, so you will almost never have accidentally the same loadout as someone else.
TF2 is one of, if not the best example of how to do a "freenium" model right. Every single weapon can be gotten without paying a cent. The only really paid stuff are cosmetics and taunts, and you can trade for those too. There are people who have started at nothing and worked up to a inventory with a value of thousands of dollars.
After a decade of existing, the game is still updated and stays in top 10 of most played games on Steam. Balance changes, cosmetics, gameplay changes etc. are still being added to the game at least twice/thrice a year in big updates.
The only problems that are quite vacant are broken comp mode (which is being worked on), hackers (which every game has) and lack of communication by VALVe (which they have improved too).

Overall, Team Fortress 2 is a great, addictive FPS. If you want to get into shooters, this is the game for you.

Team Fortress 2 is, at heart, a gloriously simple game that's been created with style, panache and an undeniable love of gaming. It's the kind of game that you want to show to people who don't play games so that they understand and then either get involved or go away. There is life before Team Fortress 2, and there is life after. After is better. Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is the sequel to the game that put class-based, multiplayer team warfare on the map. The game delivers new gametypes, a signature art style powered by Valve's next generation animation technology, persistent player statistics, and more. Unlike other "class-based" games that offer a variety of combat classes only, Team Fortress 2 packs a wild variety of classes which provide a broad range of tactical abilities and personalities, and lend themselves to a variety of player skills. Play as the flame-throwing Pyro, the room clearing Heavy, or the Spy, a master of disguises. Other classes include: Scout, Sniper, Medic, Engineer, Demoman, or Soldier.
Team Fortress 2 was first included with the release of Half-Life 2's Orange Box. Now, each game from that pack is available as its own boxed title for gamers to pick and choose their favorites.

Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is the sequel to the game that put class-based, multiplayer team warfare on the map. The game delivers new gametypes, a signature art style powered by Valve's next generation animation technology, persistent player statistics, and more. Unlike other "class-based" games that offer a variety of combat classes only, Team Fortress 2 packs a wild variety of classes which provide a broad range of tactical abilities and personalities, and lend themselves to a variety of player skills. Play as the flame-throwing Pyro, the room clearing Heavy, or the Spy, a master of disguises. Other classes include: Scout, Sniper, Medic, Engineer, Demoman, or Soldier.
Team Fortress 2 was first included with the release of Half-Life 2's Orange Box. Now, each game from that pack is available as its own boxed title for gamers to pick and choose their favorites.

Aren't you glad Team Fortress 2 didn't wind up looking like this? Valve has created quite a game with the long-awaited Team Fortress sequel, bearing many similarities to its predecessor, though incorporating enough changes to make it feel fresh. The most obvious aspect, which you may have noticed from any of the screens and video posted, is the visual style. Even after getting sucked into probably too many hours of play in the beta over the past few weeks, we're still amazed at the art design, both in how it looks and how it animates.
But let's not get too carried away with the graphics. It's a game, after all, and the most important factor is how it plays and if it's entertaining. It's interesting to see both Team Fortress 2, which has been in development on and off for some seven years now, and Splash Damage's Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, which has seen its own share of setbacks and delays, finally come out right around the same time. Their nearly simultaneous retail release presents and interesting situation for you, the consumer, as to how to spend your cash. You may fondly remember your days in Return to Castle Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, dropping air strikes on hapless attackers and eagerly charging into bunkers to spout forth deadly plumes of flamethrower fuel. Yet you can't forget your days with Team Fortress Classic, or even further back with the original Team Fortress Quake mod, with its now painfully dated character models but compelling team-focused online play.

Team Fortress must be reviewed for what it is, not what it was. The game no longer receives regular updates. You're not likely to see much change in its variety if you start playing now, but that's not the worst part. MP games require constant balance changes from developers in order to prevent exploitive gameplay and Valve shows no intent to do this.
The last update this game received was the matchmaking update more than a year ago followed by a few patches that barely improved its performance. The problem was that they introduced a new matchmaking server that was overloaded first day and blocked access for most users. That's a big failure for a company known for operating a vast network for games distribution, but maybe Akamai handles all that for them. Since then there have been no updates even though they promised an update soon after this one, the next Pyro update. The promise was made, but no deadline was given. No messages on its progress have been delivered to the community either for over a year. The closest to any information given was a developer post spitballing possible balance changes that made no mention of the Pyro update and aswell did not give a deadline for the balances to be implemented.
Valve has historically been very closed off from its customer base, this isn't new. What's new is my realization that this is unacceptable from a game developer. There are people who believe that Valve is an open work environment where employees choose what to work on and when. Even if the public relations lie was true, businesses still set deadlines. That there has been no delivery of promised content without a single post to explain its progress for over a year can only be explained by Valve never setting deadlines for it.
Despite the lack of updates, TF2 still makes alot of money for Valve. TF2 charges money for all "Special" cosmetic content which is unlike most other F2P games. If you want a killstreak weapon it will cost money. A gun that tracks kills? Money. A hat that tracks points? Money. No other way. And the cost is quite high for both methods of acquiring this content. The first method has you spin a roulette wheel by opening a crate for almost $3. But the minimum steam wallet purchase amount is $5, so you effectively pay $5 for each crate opening. The other method is just buying the items you want on the community market. The horrendously inflated community market. You want the "Nice" items? You want to spend $20 or more for them? Valve will get a cut from each purchase. They profit from the unfair crate system and overpriced market sales. You will only lose money for items you'll likely regret buying even if you're still playing this game a year later.
There are games made by other developers on Steam which promise updates and to communicate to their player base only to not deliver their promises and barely keep the game running so to make profit from it. Some of those developers run in game stores to make more money from the players. Valve is one of these developers.

Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is the sequel to the game that put class-based, multiplayer team warfare on the map. The game delivers new gametypes, a signature art style powered by Valve's next generation animation technology, persistent player statistics, and more. Unlike other "class-based" games that offer a variety of combat classes only, Team Fortress 2 packs a wild variety of classes which provide a broad range of tactical abilities and personalities, and lend themselves to a variety of player skills. Play as the flame-throwing Pyro, the room clearing Heavy, or the Spy, a master of disguises. Other classes include: Scout, Sniper, Medic, Engineer, Demoman, or Soldier.
Team Fortress 2 was first included with the release of Half-Life 2's Orange Box. Now, each game from that pack is available as its own boxed title for gamers to pick and choose their favorites.

As a near whole, FPS games aren't the bottom of the barrel, but they are the rat that tries to scrounge up ideas once everything is gone. That is, if your name is not Team Fortress 2.
Or at least that's what the community says, but I'm speaking from my perspective, not all of yours. Don't worry, I do love this game.
At its core, it is an FPS game, but the difference is that TF2 has 9 different kinds of gameplay in the form of the classes. Each is special, in how they play, and also their personalities (which is usually missing from shooters as a whole). With such a diverse spectrum of gameplay styles, players are guaranteed to find what they are looking for. The classes cover explosive power, high DPS, healing, sniping, stabbing enemies in the back, close-range powerhouse shots and flames, so it isn't hard to find a player's proficiency. All 9 characters are also absolute gems to listen too, each with an overblown stereotype and their own brand of goofiness to lighten the mood (my favourites are Demoman, Spy and Heavy). It's not often that a shooter makes you laugh, so gold star for that.
With so many ways to customize your loadout, TF2 gives a strong sense of freedom in how you look and play, and that's something that we as gamers enjoy. It allows us to feel like we have substantial control over our game, and it helps us to appreciate the progress we make, as we unlock more death toys to splatter our opponents with.
The gamemodes are a load of fun too. One of the first things I noticed was that there is no Team Deathmatch, a popular main gamemode for shooters like Call of Duty. Instead, we have Control Points (similar to Domination or Conquest), Capture the Flag (and Mannpower), Mann vs Machine (think COD Zombies, but with upgradable weapons and ROBOTS), and my personal favourite, Payload (One team pushes the cart to the end, other team tries to stop them in the time limit). All are fun to play once you understand them well enough to do well.
There are downsides to this game, however. I think the community is too 'in love' with this game to see its faults, but I see it differently. I guess it shouldn't come as a surprise that problems are what I see first in a game, and it bothers me that there is little that players can do to get the developers to work on these problems.
-Some weapons have received buffs since the release of Tough Break (Need I mention the Phlogistinator?), upsetting the balance in favour of the people using these weapons.
-VAC keeps the most well-known hacks away, but like technology, hackers are constantly evolving and adapting, so they'll come up with new cheats to show off their lack of prowess. Examples of this include shooting player through walls (Wall/Barrier hack) and seeing fully cloaked spies before they even turn a corner (I call it Spy-Vision). Valve's anti-cheat system works ok, but it can't be expected to keep up with hackers, and while this can't really be helped, it is annoying for everyone.
-Loadouts shown in the killcams can have false labelling (ex: A Sniper Rifle being labelled as a Shotgun). Not a big deal, but it's definitely a something that bugs me at least a little. I'm in no hurry to see it fixed though, as it doesn't hinder the gameplay. It's just an annoying discrepancy.
All of these issues and more have turned up recently, and the sad part is that the devs are unlikely to get around to it any time soon, if at all. Granted, there is a bug report feature, but the question of how often devs check these, and more importantly, make a worthwhile update, is still left unanswered.
Bottom line, I do like this game, but I've grown apart from it thanks to some of the recent issues. I love the characters, I love that Valve tried something different with the most uncreative genre in the history of gaming (right underneath Puzzle), and I love the diversity in gameplay, but what bugs me is that TF2 used to be a part of my daily computer time, and now I've found other things to do that are less maddening than being murdered by Soldiers with Spy-Vision. Give it some time to get their act together, and I won't have to permanently switch to Overwatch.
Final Mark: 4/5

Joke Review: Well, I have now over 1.5k hours on this game. What am I doing? Well simply, I'm just played the game. And 99% of that was opening CS:GO style crates while trying to get a Lord Gaben Weapon. 10/10 Would Recommended again IGN Masterpiece.
Serious Review: Well, I have now over 1.5k hours on this game. This game is truly what a multiplayer game should be like; a variety of weapons, 9 classes to choose from, and lots of maps. And forget mods. Yes mods. The 9 classes are Scout, Soldier, Pyro, Demoman, Heavy. Engineer, Medic, Sniper, and last but not least spy. Each class has it's own strengths and weaknesses, but all of them benefit to the team in some way. Hence this is why every class should work together as it is called TEAM Fortress 2. Not Show-off Fortress 2 (if your one of those unusual persons that have unusuals to show off....). The workshop has amazing creators creating new items everyday and Valve accepts only the best ones voted by the community. The mods in this game are pretty amazing too; you can just mod about anything, sounds, hats, weapons, the HUD, etc. This game also has weapon skins, similar to CS:GO. I'm sure Valve was running out of ideas, but hey this is a F2P game and they need more ways to make some money. I'd have to say though, these skins are damn right beautiful. The Purple Range Sniper Rifle, The Aqua Marine, they all look cool. Last but not least, the community. I'd have to say these people are dedicated to TF2, making artwork, making GMOD or SFM videos about TF2, and the youtubers such as Shibby, Muselk, STAR_, and Jerma providing TF2 videos for the communnity of TF2. Heck, once this game finally dies, everyone will be sad but if it does, then this game will go down as one of the best games in video game history. Especially in the multiplayer section. I dont think it will die out anytime soon, just look at the daily players per a day. 65k to 85k? That is a lot for a multiplayer game like this. Thanks Team Fortress 2. We'll keep on playin.

This is the core of what any succesful free-to-play game should be.  Yes you can buy stuff from the store to improve your chances, but these items (if you want them) can be earned or "found" even crafted.  This model is superb and no one can ever dare say pay-to-win.  The game requires teamwork to prevail rather than individual skill.
There are tons of different maps/modes to play.  Never a problem finding servers to play on, with a large community of people playing in countries all over the world.  I think a lot of people will agree that this is one of the best free-to-play games out there if not the best Free FPS you can find.
If you are new and are struggling to catch up to the pace and flow of the game - try using a spy class so you can become invisible.  This helped me become somewhat threatening with all classes, not just as a spy.
Not much more to say other than to those who are trying to create ANY F2P online game - forcing people into buying anything in a F2P will work only on a few.  Giving the option (however hard or diffucult to achieve) to earn anything or everything, that works for everyone.

This is a well made, stylized, team based first person shooter. Teamwork is needed to win at higher levels of play, though lone wolfing is fine on lower skill levels such as on most public servers. There are 9 classes to choose from. Each class has unique weapons and abilities that allow each to fill a unique roll as part of a larger team. This provides for a challenging and rewarding experience when faced against opponents of similar or better skill levels.
There are two official modes of play: player versus player and 'Mann Versus Machine'.
Player versus player is a mode where one team of players battles against another team of players. Within this mode, there are different types of maps. Each type of map has it's own objectives for both teams to achieve.
'Mann Verses Machine' is a mode where a team of up to 6 players battles against waves of bots. Players collect money from destroyed bots. The money is divided equally among players in the team and can be used to purchase upgrades and abilities for the next wave of bots. The pay to play sub-mode, "Mann Up", gives rewards upon completing a "tour".
In addition to the official modes of play, there are several player made mods that introduce other modes of play such as 'Versus Saxton Hale', where a team of players battles against a player playing as a character named Saxton Hale; 'Dodge Ball', where two teams of players playing as Pyros must airblast rockets and other projectiles back and forth in order to stay alive; 'Zombie Mod', where a team of players must make it to the end of the map without dying to zombies that are played by other players; to name just a few of the many player made mods available.
In addition to game play, players will randomly receive free items from the game. Some of the free items given out are weapons, hats and crates. Hats can be worn by a class to change the appearance of that class. Crates can be opened with a key. Keys can be purchased from the Mann Co Store or from the Steam Community Market or traded for from another player. Most crates will list which items can be found within them.
The game has several communities for a player to choose from if a community is what you are looking for. The game is easy to pick up and play, either alone or with friends, yet has a depth of play that will keep you from becoming bored too quickly. The dynamics between the different classes, weapons, play styles, skill levels, modes and maps provides content for many hours of play.

This is a well made, stylized, team based first person shooter. Teamwork is needed to win at higher levels of play, though lone wolfing is fine on lower skill levels such as on most public servers. There are 9 classes to choose from. Each class has unique weapons and abilities that allow each to fill a unique roll as part of a larger team. This provides for a challenging and rewarding experience when faced against opponents of similar or better skill levels.
There are two official modes of play: player versus player and 'Mann Versus Machine'.
Player versus player is a mode where one team of players battles against another team of players. Within this mode, there are different types of maps. Each type of map has it's own objectives for both teams to achieve.
'Mann Verses Machine' is a mode where a team of up to 6 players battles against waves of bots. Players collect money from destroyed bots. The money is divided equally among players in the team and can be used to purchase upgrades and abilities for the next wave of bots. The pay to play sub-mode, "Mann Up", gives rewards upon completing a "tour".
In addition to the official modes of play, there are several player made mods that introduce other modes of play such as 'Versus Saxton Hale', where a team of players battles against a player playing as a character named Saxton Hale; 'Dodge Ball', where two teams of players playing as Pyros must airblast rockets and other projectiles back and forth in order to stay alive; 'Zombie Mod', where a team of players must make it to the end of the map without dying to zombies that are played by other players; to name just a few of the many player made mods available.
In addition to game play, players will randomly receive free items from the game. Some of the free items given out are weapons, hats and crates. Hats can be worn by a class to change the appearance of that class. Crates can be opened with a key. Keys can be purchased from the Mann Co Store or from the Steam Community Market or traded for from another player. Most crates will list which items can be found within them.
The game has several communities for a player to choose from if a community is what you are looking for. The game is easy to pick up and play, either alone or with friends, yet has a depth of play that will keep you from becoming bored too quickly. The dynamics between the different classes, weapons, play styles, skill levels, modes and maps provides content for many hours of play.

Before I found Team Fortress 2, I didn't really like first-person shooters that much. With the oversaturation of half-baked, gritty and unoriginal games that seems to flood the shelves every year, I deemed the genre "not for me" and just brushed it aside.
That's where TF2 shines; it's not your younger brother's fps. It's accessable, it's diverse, it's colorful (don't confuse this for childish, it's still an M-Rated game), it has hilarious, memorable characters and a surprisingly deep backstory. It's free to install and play, and it still recieves major updates to this day after being around for eight whole years.
The nine classes and the multitude of weapons ensure that everybody finds their favorite playstyle. Want an accessable and powerful class with a rewarding skill ceiling? Want to run fast, dodge and ambush? Want to put your stealth and acting skills to the test and take out the enemy from within? Want to sit around and guzzle beer as your machines do all the killing for you? Go right ahead.
So, would I recommend it? Yes, indubitably YES. I have had far too many great experiences and memories from this game that it would be a shame for anyone to miss out.
One problem I have with this game is that, apart from the expanded inventory you get from buying your first item from the Mann Co. Store, it's generally not worth it to spend money on this game. More than likely, the key that you just bought is more valuable than what's in the box you're trying to open.

Longevity is tough for competitive shooters. Hardly a month goes by without new virtual arenas cropping up and enticing you into some fresh conflict, and only a few popular games manage to sustain active player bases even a year after their initial release. And then there's Team Fortress 2. Released in 2007, this class-based classic is still going strong well into its seventh year, thanks largely to its lively and creative community. Since GameSpot's original TF2 review, the game has benefited from numerous updates and made the jump to a free-to-play business model. So how well is Team Fortress 2 faring in 2014 among the current crop of competitors for your time and money?
The short answer is, it's holding up very well. The core action pits two teams of players against each other in a battle to capture points, move a cart, or steal a briefcase. The objective is always very straightforward; it's the interplay between the nine playable classes that makes things so varied and interesting. The speedy scout, the militant heavy, the diligent engineer, the conniving medic, the pesky sniper, the sneaky spy, the feisty pyro, the explosive soldier, and the even-more-explosive demoman all have unique weapons, attributes, and abilities that complement each other and clash in myriad ways. Encounters can vary widely depending on the match type and the makeup of each team, and this unpredictability is crucial to TF2's long-standing appeal.
When you come out of the gate as a heavy with a medic in tow, you're a formidable offensive force, but if a spy loops around to backstab the medic and you round the corner on a pyro, it can all come undone in a matter of seconds. Snipers can cover expected enemy paths, but rocket-jumping soldiers have a knack for finding alternative routes and raining explosive death from above. You may think you have a comparatively weak scout dead to rights, only to be stunned by a baseball and beaten to death. As you watch your giblets splatter on the ground and see a freeze-frame of your gleeful killer, it's hard not to chuckle at the sheer variety of ways you can meet an untimely demise. And the humorous quips, ridiculous outfits, and histrionic announcer help cultivate this lighthearted tone.
Of course, this core dynamic has persisted for most of TF2's life span, so if you stopped playing it a few years ago and come back for a few matches, you'll find things are very familiar. Learning the ropes and getting the hang of your chosen role is still a gratifying experience, and mastering advanced techniques doesn't just make you deadlier; it gives you more options for how to approach combat. Keeping your options open is still valuable too, because being flexible with your choice of character can help you avoid ending up on a catastrophically imbalanced squad. It is Team Fortress, after all.
But though there is much that has remained constant about the core game, there have been some notable changes over the years, as well as regular infusions of new weapons and items. Of the hundreds of things available in the online store, some can be unlocked through play, while others must be purchased with actual money. From small doodads that cost less than a dollar to massive bundles that cost hundreds, there's a wide range of ways to customize your experience.
Many of the items offer nothing more than a playful twist on the game's already cheeky cartoon aesthetic. You can buy hats, shirts, shoes, and other cosmetic gear to dress up like a character from Adult Swim or don spooky seasonal garb that you can wear only during Halloween or a full moon. Even if you don't fancy shelling out for any of this stuff, it's fun to see some visual variety as you try to light your opponents on fire.
Other weapons have more of an impact, like the ones that give your character a new chargeable and expendable power. The scout can build hype, which turns his usual double jump into a triple, quadruple, or quintuple jump, and the soldier can build rage, which allows him to rally his nearby teammates to do extra damage. Skills like these have more of a meaningful impact on the action, bringing something new to the table that your enemies must contend with. And then there are the totally out-there loadouts, like the one that turns the grenade-launching demoman into an extra from the movie Braveheart.In addition to the cosmetic options, there are a lot of weapons and items that offer small buffs or subtle tweaks to your attributes. Depending on which healing gun the medic equips, for example, he can imbue himself and his targeted ally with extra damage resistance or enable himself to match the speed of his target. Differences like these don't do much to change the core action, but they do give experienced players substantial room for strategic variation.
These options broaden the field of viable strategies, which helps keep combat lively and varied. And fortunately, none of the purchasable weapons or items tip the scales unfairly towards those willing to pay. Buffs and bonuses usually come with caveats, and the weapons that bestow new abilities are usually unlocked for free. For this review, I spent some money on goofy hats and some of the stranger weaponry on offer, like the pyro's flamethrower that actually shoots bubbles and rainbows. It was fun to play with the new gear, but I still found myself switching my loadout between free and paid weapons regularly to adapt to the match situation.

Snipers can cover expected enemy paths, but rocket-jumping soldiers have a knack for finding alternative routes and raining explosive death from above. You may think you have a comparatively weak scout dead to rights, only to be stunned by a baseball and beaten to death. As you watch your giblets splatter on the ground and see a freeze-frame of your gleeful killer, it's hard not to chuckle at the sheer variety of ways you can meet an untimely demise. And the humorous quips, ridiculous outfits, and histrionic announcer help cultivate this lighthearted tone.
Of course, this core dynamic has persisted for most of TF2's life span, so if you stopped playing it a few years ago and come back for a few matches, you'll find things are very familiar. Learning the ropes and getting the hang of your chosen role is still a gratifying experience, and mastering advanced techniques doesn't just make you deadlier; it gives you more options for how to approach combat. Keeping your options open is still valuable too, because being flexible with your choice of character can help you avoid ending up on a catastrophically imbalanced squad. It is Team Fortress, after all.
But though there is much that has remained constant about the core game, there have been some notable changes over the years, as well as regular infusions of new weapons and items. Of the hundreds of things available in the online store, some can be unlocked through play, while others must be purchased with actual money. From small doodads that cost less than a dollar to massive bundles that cost hundreds, there's a wide range of ways to customize your experience.

While I would suggest this game, the community, the balacing and the mildy annoying things that build up over the course of your play time, makes it so I cannot. The community is comprised of rude, childish, and often toxic people who go above and beyond to suck all enjoyment out of the game. If you're a spy and you argue with someone on your team, they'll often follow you around just to give you away. Weapons are a huge part of the game, but while playing it's evident what guns aren't well thought out. Gunslinger, Natasha and Force-O-Nature are the three main weapons that convey this idea the most. The Engineer being a defensive class, built around assisting a team with his massive turrets and moving them closer to the action via teleporters. This is broken when someone elects to use the Gunslinger, a mini sentry that can be erected in a matter of seconds for a measly amount of metal. This makes the Engineer an offensive and selfish class, running headlong into the fray to plop down a mini sentry instead of assisting the attacking team with a forward base to teleport into. The Natasha for the heavy is a minigun that slows targets as it hit's them, it's main purpose is to slow and kill Scouts easier, but it's more effective against other classes. This is in due to other classes being slower, when hit by a Natasha, it makes most classes Immobile. Finally there's the Force-O-Nature, A Double Barrel shotgun for the Scout that when shot, it pushes enemies it hits backwards. This is both disorienting and broken, as often upon spawning, you'll spawn in the ground.
This is clearly a game that Valve views more as a money maker than an actual game.

Team Fortress 2 is the highest caliber of first-person shooting action. Did I say first-person shooter? Sorry, I meant violent dress-up game. TF2 is a shooter that focuses more on cosmetic items than weapons. Much of the content is fan-created, with only occasional interruption by Valve. Also, you can get the game for 65 cents CAN by getting the free version, then buying a Sandvich from the store. The only thing you get from the full purchase is a hat. This may or may not be worth your time.
THE GOOD:
-High quality multiplayer modes
-9 fantastic characters with 27 fantastic weapons
-Model and texture quality is outstanding
-Fine power balance
-Hundreds of different weapons
-Thousands of hats
-Community is very nice
-Game can run okay even on old computers
-Not THAT violent compared to other games on the market
THE BAD:
-Negligible single player mode
-AI is very dumb
-Game is prone to glitches
-Unable to play without internet
-Only runs well on good computers; lags like a **** on others
THE UGLY:
-Almost no official content in years
-Fan base can be prone to griefing
Overall: 8/10
While TF2 may not be the greatest game ever, there is a wide world of fun and adventure to be had if you can look past its faults.

This game is possibly the most fair game. You may think "Oh, this gun is OP! I can kill everyone!" But in all reality there are always downsides, and every single weapon that has something good, also has a bad. Take the Cow Mangler 5000, ( I believe that is what it's called? ) it has unlimited ammo, and has a secondary shot that crits people and sets them on fire, almost instantly killing them, but the downside is that it does next to no damage to anything related to a building, like a sentry or a dispenser, so while you can kill people easily, that sentry can murder you in a heartbeat. Well, you may think, "Oh that isn't very bad of a downside." Okay, but if the other team has like 3 engineers, you'll get your rear handed to you on a silver plate.
Now, skill-wise, this game requires skill, and tactics, somtimes even teamwork. Even if that means you run into the other team's base just to throw milk at them (Yes, you can throw milk) just so the heavy behind you can kill the milked enemies to gain health, so he doesn't die.
For the reputation that the game has, yes its a tradefest. You could make a lot of money on steam by playing the game, if you're good.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, the company, Valve (or volvo, as some say), may have had some bumps along the road, but they're slowly starting to give the game over to the community. Is that a good choice? HELL FOCKIN' NO! HAVE YOU SEEN HOW MANY PEOPLE ON WORKSHOP POST♥♥♥♥♥♥LIKE A DICKHAT? WOOO I HAVE A DICKHAT, LOOK AT ME I'M A COMPLETE BADASS (moron). But in all seriousness, its a good idea, that way we can only blame the community for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that's happened in the past 15 years or so.

The game has improved in performance since my last review, but I still experience some of the same old problems; however, servers aren't as laggy, and they don't cause my computer to crash as often anymore.
TF2 w/ its recent updates have "improved" the game, but has created many problems:
~ If you go on a 12 vs 12 server, you have the chance of having 12 vs 7 b/c team auto balance has been removed, and you can no longer switch teams at any time unless you join a community server.
~ Some of the original maps have been removed, such as CTF Well & the map where you send the intell to a rocket.
~ None of the updates have helped w/ the community at all, and have made it slightly worse; you're more prone to false-kicking if you're not careful, and you'll have the chance of failing to connect to a server at random.
~ Back to what I said above, you may crash or not connect to a server b/c of "some reason."
~ If you're kicked once, you're permanently banned off the server.
~ Server ends as soon as the game's task is finished; i.e. Payload made it to the end, but you only have 10 or less seconds to kill people.
~ If you leave the server at all, you can never join it again.
~ Game servers that have closed are still on your saved data to revisit, but you can't revisit them.
~ The "Heavy" class has been nerfed to a point where he's super slow, and you're more better off not using him. The devs don't try to up/ buff the class at all.
~ If you send in a (bug) report, Valve will not respond even if you give them your email, same w/ feedback.
The only real thing I can say that the game has actually improved upon is performance, as in it wont lag as much or crash you as often, but that's pretty much it.
Do I recommend? Well, if you wanna deal w/ these things, go ahead, or if you want to try something free & in the FPS genre, go right ahead.

This game used to be fantastic. If you asked me to write a review about it a number of years ago I would have reccommended it. These days however it has lost its charm. Whenever I play TF2 I feel like I'm just playing a less serious version of CS:GO. The removal of being able to join and leave matches as I please was the final nail in the coffin after tier based crates that artificially changed the value of market items was a step towards this point. The only way now to get the classic TF2 experience is to play on community servers and hope you can find one without annoying plugins or unnappealing maps. They say that the bigger they are, the harder they fall and I can confirm no game fell harder than TF2. Play at your own risk.

Team Fortress 2, where do I even begin...
The trading?
The gameplay?
THE HATS?
THE CLASSES
----------------------------------------------------
There's the Scout, the Soldier, the Pyro, the Demoman, the Heavy, the Engineer, the Medic, the Sniper, and the Spy. They all have a variety of ways to either kill you easily, nearly kill you, or just annoy you to death.
The Scout is the fastest class, with his Scatterguns, Pistols, and his Bats, and he is also able to double-jump in the air.
The Soldier wields a Rocket Launcher, a Shotgun, and a Shovel, and is the second-slowest class.
The Pyro wields a Flamethrower, a Shotgun, and a Fire Axe, and is a mysterious person, whose gender is still unknown.
The Demoman wields a Grenade Launcher, Stickybomb Launcher, and a Bottle, and is a man whose liver should have shriveled up and died years ago from his drinking.
The Heavy wields a Minigun, a Shotgun, and since he is oh so manly, his bare Fists, and he is also the slowest class.
The Engineer has a Shotgun, a Pistol, and a Wrench. He is able to build Sentry Guns, Dispensers, and Teleporters, to help attack the enemy team and support his team.
The Medic wields a Syringe Gun, a Medigun, and a Bonesaw. He's a medical "expert", and his Mediguns can heal the team and Ubercharge them, which can make them invulnerable for a short period of time.
The Sniper wields a Sniper Rifle (no surprise there), an SMG (submachine gun), and a Kukri (a big knife thingy). He's Australian, he's got his sights on you, and you're his next target.
Finally, we have The Spy. French. Elegant. Sneaky. A lady-killer metaphorically and a literal man-killer. He has his Revolver, his Knife, and his Sapper, which he can use to destroy the Engineer's buildings. His Knife can kill any enemy in the game with a Backstab (do I need to explain what a BACK-STAB is?), unless they are Ubercharged or if a Sniper is wearing the Razorback, which blocks backstabs.
**NOTE: These are just stock weapons! There are tons of different weapons for you to try out! Mix and match, baby!**
THE GAMEPLAY
----------------------------------------------------
Team Fortress 2 is often times a very fun, competitive game where you can snipe, stab, shoot, or stun, through different weapons and different classes (talked about above). There are often "two groups" of TF2, the P2Ps (Pay to Plays) and F2Ps (Free to Plays). P2Ps are often known for having many cosmetics, valuable weapons, and skill, while F2Ps are often dismissed as terrible players who understand nothing and just happen to chase you around the map thinking you're a Spy. (My personal experience is that most F2Ps I meet are actually quite good players.) With many maps, many gamemodes, and many players, you're bound to have a good time. Why not try some cp_powerhouse, or maybe ctf_doublecross? Perhaps pl_bananabay?
-What is Competitive Matchmaking?-
Competitive Matchmaking means that you're put in a server with other players as good as you, like in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. This was much requested by the community as many players end up being the only good player in a server filled with terrible players, or players much much better than you. Prayers were answered in the Gun Mettle update with the introduction of matchmaking!
UPDATES
----------------------------------------------------
Team Fortress 2 is sadly being slowly updated, but these new updates often come in with the big guns. Some of the more recent updates as of January 1st, 2018 are the Smissmas 2017 Update and Jungle Inferno Update. There are also other major game updates from the past, especially the Uber Update, Love and War update and the Mann vs. Machine update. Many of these updates often have a Source Filmmaker (SFM) video to introduce these updates and their features, such as the Meet the Medic video for the Uber Update, the Expiration Date video for the Love and War update, and the leaked Invasion video for the Invasion Update. Some updates instead get a comic, such as the Gun Mettle update. Some of these events only last for a period of time and aren't permanent.
-What do these updates introduce?-
Some of these updates, in particular ones like the Love & War and Uber updates, introduce bulk amounts of new items like cosmetics, weapons, and other items like paint for your hats and unusual effects to look good in! Up until the Jungle Inferno Update, no new weapons had been added since the Tough Break updated in *2015*!

for the casual gamer the base game has a great server variety. Valve servers are very unpredictable as for the skill spread, but the Community servers are a safe bet for a more consistent skill spread (higher than on Valve servers - PUBs). The game as a whole is very easy to get into, and can be taken to the Nth degree as one pleases. Please keep in mind that the nature of the game will cause you to spend more time playing than you would think. Liken it to playing any fast-paced MMO/game. I would highly reccomend buying this game, most people are turned off due to its high price of $100 (canadian currency), but I can assure you that after completing this game, you will master the ability to carve a pumpkin with precise and quick movements using your wrist. Now I know there will be many that are skeptical after trying other products and coming up empty handed in the field of carving pumpkins, but those other products/other means of education are inferior compared to the strategies within this game that is taught thoroughly without this indie title. They have many different methods used to cover many grounds of different speeds of learning. They will allow you to master the old, and learn the new. The learning exercises are not 'one for all' method, or style, they give quite a wide variety to better suit what you want to learn and what you want to be capable of, which I find very good for my mix-match of strengths and weaknesses in specific fields.
Now you may be asking yourself: "But what else is there to learn other than the basics? How would I be able to get back into this type of craft, if Ive been out of the game for so long?" Well, the art of pumpkin carving is quite simple to get the hang of, inexperienced, or a life time carver. You just have to ease youself back into it.

I have over 1.5k hours in this game and still that is considered "decent" skill level, the skill ceiling in this game is like the distance from Earth to the Sun.  I personally like casual after MYM (maybe because I don't have the New/Different = Bad mentality.)
The game's artistic design makes it (most of the time) easy to distinguish players from background.  And some people do say the game is "pay 2 win because you have to pay money to get the items." But considering you can get the items just from playing the game anyway, and the weapons are also sidegrades, with a significant up and down, it really doen't make the game P2W (and if you really want to pay to get the items, just use the market, I mean $10.00 for a cow mangler, no thank you.)  Actually... the game might even be pay to lose! I mean think about it this way, would it be easier to spot an all stock soldier in the shadows, or a bright pink/lime green soldier with beams coming out of his head and weapon?
And you'll almost never run out of stuff to do in this game!  Even if you do get play through all of over 100 maps (some made by the community) (here is a list
) with the gamemodes: Payload, Control Points (standard, medieval and domination), Capture the Flag, King of the Hill, Payload Race, Attack/Defend, Mannpower, PASS Time, Special Delivery, Player Destruction, Arena, and Territorial Control, there is still the near infinate custom gamemodes on community servers ranging from racing giant baloons, to fighting a shirless austrailian man 1v23.

First of all, this review is coming from someone with 111 hours of TF2 so far. Not saying that is a good thing or a bad thing, but keep it in mind. This game is a Free to Play, First Person Shooter made with cartoonish graphics and a playful, less serious style. Even so, there is violence, which can potentially deter younger kids (yay) from playing. This game features matches between two different teams of players, each of which can choose one of nine classes to play as, that work together with their teams to complete the objective of the match. Different game modes have different objectives, such as trying to capture control points while the other team is defending them, moving a payload through a map, delivering the "Flag" to your team's base and more. Each of these game modes require different strategies and tactics and most importantly, teamwork, to complete the objective and beat the opposing team.
Each class has access to different kinds of weapons, including anything from Rocket Launchers to Flamethrowers and even things like powerful sentry turrets and illogical mediguns that SHOOT healing. Many classes have distinct strong points and weaknesses, and each are good for their own reasons, but the main reason why this game is so fun and enjoyable, is the amount of combinations of weapons you can equip to wreak havoc on the other team. From backstabbing them to filing them with 200 rounds of minigun ammo, there is the right playstyle for any elite mercenary. The thing that customises classes even further however, is the hats and cosmetics available in-game. These are purchased with real life money (save a few achievement cosmetics) but really go to show how much you invest in the game. If you are running around with a ghostly gibus and pyrovision goggles (for those of you who don't know, that means noob) then people are gonna know you are a 'filthy casual', but if you are running around with a unusual hats and strange killstreak weapons, people are gonna know you are the 'real deal'.
On to the money side of things. Many games are Free to Play, but even so, the developers have put time and effort into this game, so they add in some ways that they can make profit from it. Real life money can be spent on almost anything from new guns, to rare hats and apparel. All of the weapons in the game can be obtained through the random drop system and crafting, although that still requires a spot of luck to get what you want. The developers have put in an in-game store where you can buy weapons from prices ranging from about 49 cents, to $10 or so dollars. Of course, that is a tad expensive, so the even cheaper option is to buy from the Steam Community Market, where standard guns go for around 7 cents to a few dollars. The special effect guns that have cool visual images, or record kills, or record current killstreaks can go for a lot more money, especially if it is Australium. The most expensive TF2 items listed are around $400.
Because of the fact that many people can easily get sucked in and spend anywhere from a few dollars, to thousands, on this game, I recommend that you play it for a few hours and see if you like it. Don't even spend a single cent, and just see if you enjoy the gameplay. If you do, you can start to spend more time in the game, but try not to make any purchases until you are absolutely sure you want to.
Overall this game is a very addictive, easy to learn game that has a very complicated side to it whence you get far progressed.

Team Fortress 2, originally derived from years of development along with orange box, from a modification to quake multiplayer (now known as Team Fortress Classic) is a whacky, fast-paced, intelligently balanced, and high-learning-curve first person shooter multiplayer game.
It features 9 unique and complex "classes" from which to choose, each with specific talents for various situations depending on map, gameplay position, and class selections on the other team. There is scout, soldier, pyro, demoman, heavy, engineer, medic, sniper, and spy. If you learn how to play every one of these and learn what weapons and loadouts are, you will be only marginally good at the game.
To be good at this game requires something called TEAMWORK. It's a frustrating, addictive, cartoonishly funny, skillful masterpiece, which is constantly in development by its lazy developers who leave bugs all around. This game is free to play, but I would recommend paying a small amount for a cool taunt or hat, and you're on your way to becoming the mediocre slime everybody knows and loves, setting things on fire, headshotting, gibbing people, healing patients from afar, and blasting hoardes of enemies with stationary turrets. This game is your own, and there's no right or wrong way to play it. But there are MANY wrong ways if you want to win. None of the right ways don't involve teamwork and using your head. Have fun. Random critical hits are fair and balanced.

radical TF2 Player:
Once upon a time, in a magical land called (player's location), a little boy by the name of (player's name) decided to play this nonsense of a game (so he thought!) called Team Fortress 2. The story of your
radical TF2 Player:
Once upon a time, in a magical land called (player's location), a little boy by the name of (player's name) decided to play this nonsense of a game (so he thought!) called Team Fortress 2. At first, he didn't understand the game! He saw so many people in cool hats, MLG 360 Professional Headshot only weed-smoking snipers who don't miss, and hit-every-shot scouts! Man, all he knew was the weak power of the no cosmetic stock sniper...
After 100 hours of training in this mysterious game, the boy thought he was actually so good at the game that he could be considered a MLG 360 Professional Headshot only weed-smoking sniper who doesn't miss! He bought hats, cosmetics, strange professional killstreaks, australiums, everything!
But that day, he had a rude awakening. He forgot about the real MLG 360 Professional Headshot only weed-smoking snipers who don't miss! He has recently learned this overused word... hacker. And boy did the pro show this kid. Man... the kid was raging so hard in the chat that the Professional blocked him... what do you expect? But, he told himself..."Don't let your dreams be dreams..."
From that day forth he put aside homework, friends, family, dinner... just to train at TF2. He has been tracking this pro for quite some time now. It turns out that this pro had a YouTube channel. The boy would use this pro's tips and train harder every day. When Christmas came around, he'd beg his parents to buy him a new gaming computer... and they did.
Man... did he show that he was good! He practiced the 180 quickscope trickshot everyday to the point where he only ate cold pizza, Doritos and drank Mountain Dew. He bought all the unusuals... burning flames, scorched flames, searing plasma, green energy, everything! He was the dankest TF2 player there was. Then it hit him. The Pro must go down.
He devised a clever trap to make the Pro challenge him to TF2. While the Pro would be streaming, the boy would join his game, 180 quickscope headshot him, and taunt. But that didn't do it. The Pro used the Darwin's Danger Shield. The Pro went back to the spawn locker and went the most dreaded class in all of Team Fortress 2... the scout.
But this boy has trained for this. He's practice shooting moving targets. The boy dominated the Pro, but he had another rude awakening.
He asked himself..."Why? Why put aside a life and friends for this?"
But he answered himself..."Because Gaben. Duh."

Team Fortess Two is a causal class based first person shooter which is known for its ability to place a player into a low-stress quickplay server in under 60 seconds, its humorous collection of hats and other cosmetics, and its friendy  and overall  accepting community. All of these things contributed to the unique atmosphere surrounding Team Fortress Two
.....Or at least, they used to make it unique.
In the age of toxic rage inducing "clutch or kick" competitive enviroments, and the corporate cash-grabs of micro transactions through skins, crates/loot boxes, DLCs, and the like, TF2 was an oasis in the middle of a barron waste land. Offering players a chance to hop into a Valve server in under a minute, and  play for as long or short a time as they wanted, was a welcome change of pace from the long que times and abbandonment penalties of many other games. Being able to play on a balanced team, switch from side to side, Vote kick hackers, call for a map change, and rejoin servers by using the server browser provided the grounds for a care-free and relaxing gaming experience that you could not find in other games. The only visible sign of a skill or statistic based hierarchy was TF2's wide assortment of hats. Hats represented a players experience, and distinguished players with high, or low, skill. Because there was no offical "rank" system besides hats (which are not associated with actual stats), players had no reason to feel stressed because a win or loss would effect their stats, which is why TF2 had such a relaxing and laid back enviroment that distinguished it from games that were over-competitive and toxic.
Sadly, Valve (The Developer of TF2 and many other canonical games) has gone the way of many other large game developement companies, and is now only focused on copy and pasting ideas and techniques to maximize profit, instead of coming up with new ideas and concepts. Seeing the success of games like CS:GO, and especially TF2's "competitor" Overwatch (Which shares few actual similarites with TF2), Valve decided that TF2 didn't need need to be different. People liked competitive game modes, crates/loot boxes, and skins for everthing inculding the kitchen sink in those games, why not see them in TF2? After all, portions of the TF2 comunity had been asking for competititve for an eterinity, why not imlpement them?
These additions would be received with open arms by the TF2 community...Or would they?
The Meet Your match uptate was the beggining of the end for TF2. The Meet you Match update had finally introduced a competitive game mode for TF2, which had been requested by many people for a long time. But it came at a cost. This update had fundamentaly changed TF2. Gone were the days of being able to hop into a quickplay server were now over. They were replaced by long que times, the loss of the ability to rejoin a game, and the insanity of being penalized for leaving a casual game. The addition of an offical ranking system meant that there was now a competitive edge to what was supposed to be the fun, care-free, and laid back replacement for quicklplay, casual mode. The UI was almost complety reworked aswell.
All of these changes went completely reversed the alure of TF2. Now TF2 is over-competitive, stressful, and much more toxic than it used to be. This is only made worse by the lack of care and incompetance displayed by Valve in the way that the Meet your Match update was implenented(15 min. waits for games, abandonment penelties for casual, etc.). Valve has also shown how they are trying to make TF2 like one of their other games, CS:GO, because it will increase profits through micrtransactions. Team Fortess Two is a causal class based first person shooter which is known for its ability to place a player into a low-stress quickplay server in under 60 seconds, its humorous collection of hats and other cosmetics, and its friendy  and overall  accepting community. All of these things contributed to the unique atmosphere surrounding Team Fortress Two
.....Or at least, they used to make it unique.
In the age of toxic rage inducing "clutch or kick" competitive enviroments, and the corporate cash-grabs of micro transactions through skins, crates/loot boxes, DLCs, and the like, TF2 was an oasis in the middle of a barron waste land. Offering players a chance to hop into a Valve server in under a minute, and  play for as long or short a time as they wanted, was a welcome change of pace from the long que times and abbandonment penalties of many other games. Being able to play on a balanced team, switch from side to side, Vote kick hackers, call for a map change, and rejoin servers by using the server browser provided the grounds for a care-free and relaxing gaming experience that you could not find in other games. The only visible sign of a skill or statistic based hierarchy was TF2's wide assortment of hats. Hats represented a players experience, and distinguished players with high, or low, skill. Because there was no offical "rank" system besides hats (which are not associated with actual stats), players had no reason to feel stressed because a win or loss would effect their stats, which is why TF2 had such a relaxing and laid back enviroment that distinguished it from games that were over-competitive and toxic.
Sadly, Valve (The Developer of TF2 and many other canonical games) has gone the way of many other large game developement companies, and is now only focused on copy and pasting ideas and techniques to maximize profit, instead of coming up with new ideas and concepts. Seeing the success of games like CS:GO, and especially TF2's "competitor" Overwatch (Which shares few actual similarites with TF2), Valve decided that TF2 didn't need need to be different. People liked competitive game modes, crates/loot boxes, and skins for everthing inculding the kitchen sink in those games, why not see them in TF2? After all, portions of the TF2 comunity had been asking for competititve for an eterinity, why not imlpement them?
These additions would be received with open arms by the TF2 community...Or would they?
The Meet Your match uptate was the beggining of the end for TF2. The Meet you Match update had finally introduced a competitive game mode for TF2, which had been requested by many people for a long time. But it came at a cost. This update had fundamentaly changed TF2. Gone were the days of being able to hop into a quickplay server were now over. They were replaced by long que times, the loss of the ability to rejoin a game, and the insanity of being penalized for leaving a casual game. The addition of an offical ranking system meant that there was now a competitive edge to what was supposed to be the fun, care-free, and laid back replacement for quicklplay, casual mode. The UI was almost complety reworked aswell.
All of these changes went completely reversed the alure of TF2. Now TF2 is over-competitive, stressful, and much more toxic than it used to be. This is only made worse by the lack of care and incompetance displayed by Valve in the way that the Meet your Match update was implenented(15 min. waits for games, abandonment penelties for casual, etc.). Valve has also shown how they are trying to make TF2 like one of their other games, CS:GO, because it will increase profits through micrtransactions. This is demonstrated by the addition of an aplethera of new crates, and ranked weapon skins. Take a look at TF2's new UI, even it now closely resembles that of CS:GO(freinds list, advertisements, gamemodes,etc.).
Valve has literally sold the soul of TF2 to make it more like other games, and(at least for me) the Jungle Inferno update is the last nail in the australium plated coffin of Team Fortress Two.
Here lies the grave of TF2, may its soul rest in peace.

I have played Team Fortress 2 for years now, firstly on Xbox 360 via the Orange box, and now on Steam/PC. Yet still, I can’t put it down. I always come back to it and enjoy it more and more each time I do. The lore and community made stuff really keeps this game alive and adds to the game’s charm in my opinion.  I really like how the game is free to play and that the purchased items are fair and balanced. You can play without paying for anything, and still do well competitively. The game will run well on nearly any computer, and is always operational. Never have the servers closed down stopping me from playing the game. Team Fortress 2 receives regular updates, such as new maps, game modes and items, which change up the gameplay a lot.
My only critique would be some of the player base community. Most of the players are great people and really fun to play with, proving you with a good challenge and some good laughs. But, some can be annoying, offensive and lacking in sportsmanship. This can ruin the game and give the fans a bad reputation. But overall I would recommend the game, just be prepared (as with any game really) to come across some jerks.

I find it amazing that a game with a hat economy could not survive, but thrive for 8 years with an iron-clad community backing it. Of course, it's probably because it's gone where no FPS has ever gone before. It's got funny taunts, weird cosmetics, nine completely different classes with almost bipolar roles and most of all: variety. You don't even have to stop at that; the items have different qualities. Strange, for people who like racking up stats and changing the name of the item (I have a Boxcar Bomber myself, its' rank: fancy schmancy)! There's also killstreaks for tryhards who like their name on a plaque above everyone's screen certifying that they got their 22nd kill. There are the super-rare australium drops found in the game's mann vs machine mode that are golden versions of the normal weapons. And then finally there are the highly respected items known as unusuals. You can even paint and rename stuff! Really, the only criticism I have about the game is that players can be really harsh on the new guy who's just a default heavy or whatever. My suggestion for newbies is that you stick to the training mode until you get the hang of each class, then join an actual server when you're confident in your own ability. Don't even think aout going for mvm before getting on to a really advanced playing level. So, I guess if you're getting tf2 for the first time, you're all set! Keep being awesome, Valve!

Before I got my own computer (which is nowhere near top notch. It came with windows 8 and the best thing it can run is Outlast at minimal setting), I had a crappy laptop that could barely even run RuneScape at minimal graphics.
TF2 was something I wanted to play for a long time, and it's one of the primary reasons I got a computer, but enough about me not having the game, let's talk about me HAVING the game...
Tf2, although being Free to play, it does not suffer from any of the downsides of F2P. There are no ads that cover♥♥♥♥♥♥up when you first get on, and there's no "Paying for upgrades" or any nonsense like that. The only things you can pay for are accessories and taunts, which are completely cosmetic. Guess it makes sense, being that this use to not be F2P.
I like the term "Free to start" since many "F2p" games are just ad-covered piles of pay-to-win bull crap, but TF2 is probably the only game I've played that truely deserves the name "Free to Play".
ANYWAY, right, gameplay.
Rather than being some generic, borring, zero-personality gunsman. You instead get to choose between 9 classes that all have different weapons, advantages, and weaknesses, and they all have different,  yet easy to remember voices that are hilarious and cheesy. It's also easy to reccognize what characters are what, even if they're not holding out a noticable weapon.
The gameplay is fast, moving around doesn't mess up your aiming reticule, but you do have to be quick with the mouse to be able to stop some fast moving targets.
All the official game modes are team-based, and involve capturing and/or defending a point from the other team. There's no friendly fire, so you don't have to worry about any teammates lighting you on fire or anything, just watch out for spies...

Going on 8 years and still doing very well for itself, TF2 is a testament to Valve's dedication and consistent content support across all their games. TF2 is unique because it's ostensibly undergone the biggest changes of any of Valve's other games, through hundreds of free updates. To some, that's a bad thing - that TF2's initially unique and intelligent art direction has been diluted with hats, cosmetics and things that seem to make no visual sense. But it adds layers of customization, trading and player interaction that form a remarkable metagame. The new weapons and maps have done nothing but add extra replayability and depth to the game - and it even has its own active competitive scene.
Then you have things like Mann vs Machine, the custom server community and their unique player-made mods and you have an experience that still has a lot of life in it and a seemingly endless supply of... well, game. Oh, and it's free.

What the biggest standout of this game is compared to other FPS is the classes.
Nearly every other FPS I've ever played never really covered that sort of area. In some games, you don't really have classes, but perks that slightly change your character, but in this game, with the many classes and variety, you can play different styles which helped made the game something to come back to!
And of corse, the hats are (obviously) amazing and gives the characters different styles which is nice.
Then it happened...
The "Meet your Match" update was clearly my most awaited update. I was and all my friends were really pumped for it, until we saw it.
Upsides: The main menu is a lot neater, with a better setup compared to the old version. The new smaller view models are quite nice and can be helpful and thank god passtime is out of beta! Also, it's nice that competitive has started.
Downsides: Firstly, even though the main menu is good, you can no longer make your own server, so goodbye tr_walkway, and casual is a mess. Pubs were completely fine and didn't need to be touched, but valve messed up big time and made it competitive's weird nephew. With no kicks and autoscramble, casual is the worst downside of all. And worst of all, we need to rely on community servers, which may have crappy plugins and loud ads. Thank god valve is seeing to it.
Some weapons in this update has completely changed, such as the Shortstop. This wep use to be used as a perk because of the bonus healing, but valve completely wiped it out and it now has a, uhh... pushing mechanic? Even classes got buffed, like the medic can run as fast the heal target, which I think is OK on 1 side of it, but makes him overpowering as hell. And engies only need 50 metal for a teleporter. ONLY 50.
So the recent update sucks heaps, but do I still recommend it? Surprisingly, yes. Of course it now is kinda bad, casual is slightly improving (thank god) with waiting times getting gradually faster. Let's hope it gets better from here, or goodbye tf2!

It also has a good trading community, where I met many of my friends that I still talk to today.
I highly recommend this game to anybody looking for a fun new FPS to try out.

Going on 8 years and still doing very well for itself, TF2 is a testament to Valve's dedication and consistent content support across all their games. TF2 is unique because it's ostensibly undergone the biggest changes of any of Valve's other games, through hundreds of free updates. To some, that's a bad thing - that TF2's initially unique and intelligent art direction has been diluted with hats, cosmetics and things that seem to make no visual sense. But it adds layers of customization, trading and player interaction that form a remarkable metagame. The new weapons and maps have done nothing but add extra replayability and depth to the game - and it even has its own active competitive scene.
Then you have things like Mann vs Machine, the custom server community and their unique player-made mods and you have an experience that still has a lot of life in it and a seemingly endless supply of... well, game. Oh, and it's free.
